playbook:
**Playbook for ESTATE**

Buying decisions:
- Buy aggressively in the early laps whenever I can afford it. Rent-collecting potential compounds over the remaining laps, and a deed counts at full purchase price in the final score — so an early buy roughly pays for itself plus income.
- A good rule: buy any unowned tile in laps 1–3 if the purchase leaves me with a non-negative balance. Don't skip a buy just because my cash buffer would get small; the buffer matters less than income and endgame net worth.
- In the last lap or two, only buy if the price is fully recoverable (rent plus salary still to come) — otherwise cash in hand is worth just as much as the deed.

Cash management:
- Track my true balance carefully each turn: start from my last declared balance, add salary when passing START, add any rents received "since my last turn," then subtract purchases and rent paid.
- Keep at least a rough cushion in mind so I'm not locked out of cheap tiles — I lost out on buying a 50 and a 60 tile in back-to-back laps because I'd spent nearly everything and couldn't add either to my net worth. The fix: when two or more tiles are still unowned and I have limited cash, prefer buying the tile I can actually afford *and* keep enough for the next-cheapest unowned tile — but if I can only afford one, still buy it rather than hoard.

Endgame:
- Remember the scoring: final score = declared cash + purchase prices of deeds held. Every rent I collect is pure gain; every rent I pay is a small loss but unavoidable.
- Always pay rent promptly and declare the correct balance — the books are my own responsibility and errors compound.

General principle: income-generating assets beat idle cash over a multi-lap game. When a purchase is offered and I have the money, the default answer is yes, especially early.

**Playbook for ref_estate**

- The score is cash plus purchase price of deeds held, so buying is not a cost to net worth — a fairly priced property is free equity. When an unowned tile is put to me and I have enough cash to stay solvent, I buy.
- Prefer buying early. Every lap an owned tile goes unbought is a lap of rent flowing to whoever else grabs it. When the first unowned property comes up in the early laps, I do not hesitate.
- Cheapest tiles (Depot, Quarry) give the same equity boost per lap of ownership sooner because they pay back rent faster relative to price. When choosing among unowned tiles, cheap ones first.
- I will cross START roughly once per lap for salary, so plan rent payments around that rhythm. Keep a cash buffer of at least the largest rent on the board (about 30) at all times; never spend down to where one landing bankrupts or forces sloppy declarations.
- Rents paid out are pure loss to my score. There is no way to avoid them except ownership, which is another reason to convert cash into deeds aggressively rather than hoard it — cash hoarding earned nothing here.
- Track my balance carefully each turn; declare only what the arithmetic supports, since the bank keeps its own books and discrepancies are the main way to lose a settled position.
- Do not skip a purchase late in the game on "not enough laps left" reasoning unless the tile is very expensive — even a late buy converts cash to deed value one-for-one, so it is at worst neutral on the final score and often positive.

2.text:
Final tally: cash 61 + Wharf 80 + Exchange 120 = 261 for the win. Write the playbook.

**Playbook for ESTATE**

- I track my net worth, not just cash: cash + purchase price of my deeds. A purchase doesn't cost me net worth, it converts cash to deed value. So when buying, I'm really asking whether the deed's rent stream beats holding cash — and cash earns nothing here.

- When an unowned tile is put to me and the purchase leaves me with a nonnegative balance (or nearly so), I buy. Rent-to-price ratio matters: prefer anything at or above roughly 20% (rent/price). High absolute rent is also worth paying up for, because opponents pay it to me.

- I will spend down to nearly zero on strong properties early, since salary (25/lap) refills me and the win condition counts deeds at full purchase price. Buying at 120 with 120 in hand was correct — it ended up worth +120 plus collected rents and I never went bankrupt.

- Landing on my own tile costs nothing: I just confirm balance unchanged.

- When rent is due, I pay promptly and update balance exactly, including any funds received from other investors since my last turn ("since your last turn you received N" must be added to my last declared balance).

- When my cash is below the price of an unowned tile, I decline — I cannot buy what I can't pay for, and I should say so plainly.

- I keep an eye on the bank's transfer log to gauge opponents' income flows; opponents who bought early keep collecting, so denying them tiles by buying first is worth a thin cash cushion.

- At the final lap, I make sure my declared balance is exact, since the score is computed from it.
